ds: Looting, theft, forgery and illicit trade of cultural property, and use of art as a store of value to launder funds. Opaque transactions, free ports, falsified provenance and anonymous buyers are common features.

src.t: FATF, Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing in the Art and Antiquities Market (2023)
UNESCO, Convention on the Means of Prohibiting and Preventing the Illicit Import, Export and Transfer of Ownership of Cultural Property (1970)
UNIDROIT, Convention on Stolen or Illegally Exported Cultural Objects (1995)
INTERPOL, Stolen Works of Art Database

rat: Art and antiquities dealers, auction houses and agents settle by wire or cash; artworks are stored in free ports or custody and sometimes used as loan collateral.

ind.n: Provenance gaps or documents inconsistent with object history
ind.cx: Missing ownership chain, 1970-era gap or fake certificates.
ind.ds: Missing ownership chain, 1970-era gap or fake certificates.

ind.n: Price inconsistent with market or sudden value jumps
ind.cx: Sales at far off valuations or back-to-back trades.
ind.ds: Price paid differs sharply from market value, comparable sales or estimates without commercial justification.
ind.cn: Transaction price materially different from market value

ind.n: Anonymous buyers through intermediaries, trusts or shell companies
ind.ds: Property, art, vessels or other valuables are acquired or held via a company, trust or storage arrangement with concealed beneficial owners.
ind.cn: High-value asset held through opaque vehicle

ind.n: Storage in free ports without display or trade
ind.cx: Artworks stored for long without movement.
ind.ds: Artworks are acquired and stored long term in free ports with no movement, display or documented purpose.
ind.cn: Art or collectibles held in free ports without display or trade

ind.n: Cash or crypto payment for high-value works
ind.ds: High-value assets are bought with cash, crypto, third-party or otherwise non-standard funding.
ind.cn: High-value purchases paid in cash, crypto or non-standard funds

ind.n: Objects from conflict zones or countries with looting
ind.cx: Antiquities exported from affected regions with new papers.
ind.ds: Antiquities exported from affected regions with new papers.

ind.n: Seller is dealer new to market or with sanctions or adverse media
Use of art as collateral or for loan with unclear valuations
ind.cx: Loans secured on art with inflated valuations.
ind.ds: Loans secured on art with inflated valuations.

ctl.ds: Cross-checks asset ownership, title history, security registrations and registry changes against official registers, including for changes close to designation or transaction dates. It confirms that the person presenting an asset genuinely owns it.

Obtains independent valuations, appraisals or comparable-sale evidence for high-value assets, collateral and traded goods, and escalates large variances. It reveals deliberately mispriced assets used to move or conceal value.

Requires documentary evidence of origin, legal sourcing, custody and conformity with responsible-sourcing standards, including for informal or recycled supply. It keeps illicitly sourced goods from entering the financed or traded chain.

Detects funds that return to their origin or loop between linked parties through reciprocal, matched, netted or round-trip flows using graph analysis and account comparison. It exposes artificial turnover and loan-back structures.

Identifies the natural persons who ultimately own or control a legal entity or arrangement and verifies them using independent registers and documents, looking through intermediate layers. It is the core defence against anonymity achieved through layered or opaque structures.
Risk-based vetting of intermediaries, brokers, partners and suppliers covering ownership, experience, references, public-official links and selection rationale. It limits exposure through proxies.

Applies enhanced checks to operators, counterparties, storage rationale and transactions that involve free-trade zones and free ports, including facility operator controls. It addresses the opacity and reduced oversight these locations can offer.

Prohibits or caps cash for purchases, loans, donations and settlement above a set value, requiring documented non-cash methods and threshold reporting for dealers. It removes a low-traceability payment route.

Translates published and sanitised typologies and red flags into targeted monitoring scenarios and context-aware rules that are reviewed periodically. It aligns monitoring with known criminal methods.

Blocks or refers transfers, goods, services and system access linked to embargoed or comprehensively sanctioned territories using address, route, payment-country and device-location signals. It prevents prohibited dealings from being processed.

ctl.n: Licence and permit verification for regulated goods
ctl.ds: Validates licences, permits, certificates and authorisations with the issuing authority and compares their scope with observed activity or shipments. It prevents genuine permits being misused or forged permits being accepted.

Screens customers, owners, counterparties, vessels, dealers and addresses against sanctions, enforcement and restricted-party lists at onboarding and ongoing, using fuzzy matching and secondary identifiers. Potential matches are held for adjudication before service or funds are released.

Applies targeted enhanced checks to customer types or sectors known to be vulnerable to misuse, such as cash-intensive trades, money service businesses, high-value dealers, professional services, charities or waste handlers. Questions and evidence are tailored to how the sector normally operates.
Tailors training content and frequency to role and risk for finance, relationship, underwriting and compliance staff, with feedback of quality assurance findings. It builds baseline competence.
